title: Your Post-Close Checklist: Insurance, Utilities & Handoff to Operations

slides.title: Write down everything the closing team learned before the launch team needs it
slides.subtitle: Lesson PA.12. Your Post-Close Checklist: Insurance, Utilities & Handoff to Operations
meta: Education only. Not legal, tax, or insurance advice.
slides.notes:
You own the house. This lesson turns it into something that's ready to become a rental.

After this lesson you can confirm you have the right insurance and move every utility and account into your control. You can also finish the safety work before anyone takes a photo.

The main output is a dated operations handoff packet. It tells the launch team everything the closing team learned, including what's still open.

Throughout, I follow Cedar Ridge, the course's hypothetical three-bedroom lake house. It has a dock, a private well, and septic, and it sleeps eight guests. Maya and Chris bought it with a DSCR loan, a rental loan the lender sizes mainly on the property's income. Sam records the live demos. He teaches the operations lessons, OP.1 to OP.5, that come right after this one.

The 45-day timeline is an assumption. None of this is legal, tax, or insurance advice. Your insurer, licensing office, and CPA confirm the parts that depend on your address and policy.

slides.title: The closing and launch teams rarely talk, so a written packet carries the knowledge

left.head: The closing team
left.note: Knows what's wrong with the house.
items: Agent, lender, inspector, title company, attorney
The inspector knows the dock railing is loose
The seller named the septic company at the walkthrough

right.head: The launch team
items: Insurer, cleaner, handyman, furnishing help, maybe a co-host
A listing and software setup built on what you know
The cleaner and co-host never heard any of it

box.label: The handoff packet
box.text: Every open item gets an owner and a date. You may be both teams on your first property. Write the packet anyway.

slides.notes:
Up to now, your team was the closing team. Agent, lender, inspector, title company, attorney.

Now your team is the launch team. Insurer, cleaner, handyman, furnishing help, and maybe a co-host. The listing and software setup come next, in Sam's OP.1 to OP.5.

These two teams rarely talk to each other. The inspector knows the dock railing is loose. The cleaner doesn't. The seller told you the septic company's name at the walkthrough. Your co-host will never hear it unless you write it down.

The handoff packet is how the first team's knowledge reaches the second. Every open item gets an owner and a date.

On your first property, you're probably both teams. Write the packet anyway. The version of you who's answering a guest at 11 p.m. in February needs it.

slides.title: Read your policy as the operator, checking nine items the lender never asked about
items: Named insured matches how you took title (you, your LLC, or both)
Effective date is the closing date or earlier
Covers short-term rental to paying guests, in writing
Liability limit per occurrence, including dock, water, and watercraft
Deductibles: all-perils, plus any wind, hail, or water deductible
Exclusions: slow leaks, mold, pools and hot tubs, 'business' use
Loss of rental income: when it pays, how it's calculated, for how long
Flood: your FEMA flood zone and whether you have a flood policy
Conditions the insurer set (Cedar Ridge: railing, alarms): proof sent, confirmed in writing
slides.notes:
You bought, or bound, a policy before closing, because the lender required it. Now read it as the operator. The lender cared that the house was insured. You care whether a guest injury, a burst pipe, or a month without bookings is covered.

Pull the declarations page, the summary of who's insured, the limits, and the deductibles. Pull the policy form too. Check these nine items.

The named insured has to match how you took title in PA.10. The effective date has to be the closing date or earlier. A standard homeowners policy may exclude business use, so get the insurer's answer on rental use in writing.

Check the liability limit per incident, especially for the dock and the water. Note the deductibles. Read the exclusions. Check loss-of-rental-income coverage.

And the conditions. When Maya and Chris got their quote in due diligence, the insurer required the railing and alarms within 30 days. Send proof and get written confirmation.

slides.title: AirCover may help on some Airbnb claims, so your own policy must carry the full load

left.head: What Airbnb says AirCover includes
items: Host liability insurance, plus host damage protection
Screening and a safety line
Protection while you're hosting an Airbnb stay

right.head: What Airbnb says it isn't
items: Host damage protection isn't an insurance policy
Not all damage is included
Not a substitute for your own insurance
A Vrbo or direct booking isn't an Airbnb stay

box.label: Flood has a waiting period
box.text: Most homeowners policies don't cover flood; it's a separate policy (FEMA). The National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) generally has a 30-day wait, with exceptions such as buying when you make, increase, extend, or renew a mortgage.

slides.notes:
Now the platform. Airbnb's AirCover for Hosts has two protection pieces: host liability insurance and host damage protection. It also includes screening and a safety line.

Airbnb says the damage piece, host damage protection, isn't an insurance policy, and not all damage is included. It says AirCover isn't a substitute for your own insurance, and suggests talking to your insurer about overlap.

Airbnb describes AirCover as protection while you're hosting an Airbnb stay. A guest who books on Vrbo, or on your direct site from OP.3, isn't an Airbnb stay. Your own policy has to carry the whole load. Treat AirCover as a backup that may help on some Airbnb claims.

One more on flood. FEMA says most homeowners insurance doesn't cover flood. The National Flood Insurance Program, the NFIP, generally has a 30-day waiting period, with exceptions. If you skipped flood at closing, the clock may start the day you buy.

slides.title: Move every utility and account into your name within the first week
columns: What to set up at Cedar Ridge
rows: Autopay. A propane delivery schedule so the tank never runs dry mid-stay.
No bill. Note the shutoff, pump, pressure tank, and when the UV lamp is due.
Schedule the inspection and pumping program budgeted in PA.9.
Pickup day, bin size, whether the hauler serves rentals, who brings bins out.
Fastest reliable service. Test real speed in the bedrooms. Router out of guest reach.
A unique code for each stay and each vendor. Remove the seller's codes.
Follow Airbnb's device rules. Remove any indoor camera the seller left.
Forwarding or a local box. Permit renewals and tax notices arrive by mail.
Confirm who plows a private road, and when. Contract your own if needed.
slides.caption: Use the PA.11 walkthrough meter readings so the seller's final bills and your first bills split cleanly.
slides.notes:
Transfer every account into your name, or your entity's name, within the first week. Use the meter readings you took at the PA.11 walkthrough so the bills split cleanly.

Here's the list for Cedar Ridge.

Electric and propane on autopay, with a propane delivery schedule. The well has no water bill, but it has a pump, a pressure tank, and an ultraviolet, or UV, light system that treats the water. The seller installed it before closing. Write down where the shutoff is and when the lamp is due. Schedule the septic program you budgeted.

Eight guests make more trash than a family. Confirm pickup day, bin size, and whether the hauler serves rentals.

Test the internet speed in the bedrooms, and put the router where guests can't unplug it.

The smart lock issues a unique code for each stay and each vendor. Remove the seller's codes. Then set up mail forwarding and snow plowing.

slides.title: Follow Airbnb's device rules, and keep every login in a password manager

left.head: Allowed, with rules
items: Smart home devices (Airbnb encourages you to disclose them)
Outdoor cameras, disclosed with general location before booking
Noise decibel monitors in common areas only, disclosed

right.head: Not allowed
items: Cameras that monitor indoor spaces, even if they're off
If the seller left an indoor camera, remove it

box.label: Credentials
box.text: Every login goes in a password manager with shared access. Don't email or text credentials. Turn on two-factor sign-in for utility, internet, lock, and platform accounts.

slides.notes:
Devices come with platform rules, so check them before you install anything.

Airbnb allows smart home devices and encourages you to disclose them. Outdoor cameras must be disclosed, with their general location, before booking. Noise decibel monitors are allowed only in common areas, and must be disclosed.

Airbnb doesn't allow cameras that monitor indoor spaces, even if they're turned off. If the seller left one, take it down.

Now credentials. Put every login in a password manager, with shared access for anyone who needs it. Don't email credentials or send them by text. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's closing-scam guidance warns that email isn't a secure way to send financial information. Treat account logins the same way.

Turn on two-factor sign-in for the utility, internet, lock, and platform accounts.

slides.title: Build the vendor list now, while nothing is broken
items: Cleaner ($150 per turnover, each guest changeover): intro visit before the cleaning checklist
On-call handyman ($150 monthly retainer): full walk, including dock, septic, well
Septic, well and water treatment, HVAC, and pest services from PA.9
Emergency plumber and electrician for nights and weekends
Plow service and trash hauler
Backup cleaner or local co-host for a missed clean (choosing a co-host comes later)
Local licensing office and lodging tax contact

box.label: Vendor access
box.text: Give each vendor their own lock code, and delete it when the job ends. Record who has a physical key, if anyone does.

slides.notes:
Your vendor list is the difference between a two-hour fix and a cancelled stay. Build it now, while you're calm.

The Cedar Ridge budget pays the cleaner $150 a turnover. A turnover is the clean between one guest leaving and the next arriving. Set up an intro visit before OP.8 builds the cleaning checklist, the SOP.

The budget also pays a $150 monthly retainer to an on-call handyman or inspector. Walk them through the whole house, including the dock and the septic and well equipment.

Most of the specialists came out of due diligence: septic, well and water treatment, heating and cooling, and pest. Add an emergency plumber and electrician who answer nights and weekends. Add the plow service and the trash hauler.

Have one backup name for a missed clean. OP.7 covers the bigger choice between a cleaner, a co-host, or a property manager.

Give each vendor their own lock code and delete it when the job ends.

slides.title: File the permit and lodging tax registration before the first stay

nodes.d: Cedar Ridge's permit didn't transfer, so they apply as new owners.
Separate from the permit. Part One lesson 3.3 covers collecting it.
Don't publish first if local rules require the permit.
Airbnb's laws and regulations section. Sam's OP.1 builds the listing.

box.label: Your local-rules checklist (SR.1)
box.text: Your local-rules checklist (SR.1) records the exact rule and the date you checked it. Bring the permit number and exact holder name to Sam's OP.1.

slides.notes:
Diligence told you whether this address can run a rental. Now you file.

For Cedar Ridge, PA.9 found the seller's permit doesn't transfer. So Maya and Chris apply as new owners on day 2.

The same day, they register for lodging and occupancy tax. That's separate from the permit. Register with the state or local tax agency before your first stay. Lesson 3.3 in Part One shows how collection works on each booking channel.

Then you wait. Don't publish a listing before the permit is issued if the local rules require the permit first. Your local-rules checklist, resource SR.1, records the exact rule and when you checked it.

When the permit number comes back, Airbnb has a field for it. It sits under the listing's policies and rules, in the laws and regulations section. Sam's OP.1 shows listing setup across platforms. Bring the permit number and the exact holder name.

slides.title: Finish the safety work before photos, because photos set what guests expect

box.label: Cedar Ridge sign-off
box.text: One-page sign-off: item, who checked, date, photo. Both groups finish before photos.

slides.notes:
Don't photograph a house you haven't finished fixing. Photos lock in what guests expect, and a listing can't promise a dock that isn't safe yet.

Start with the punch list from due diligence. Then walk the house against Airbnb's safety requirements. Airbnb says hosts must disclose whether smoke and carbon monoxide detectors are present. If they are, they must work and be tested. Its hazard list includes blocked exits, exposed wiring, contaminated water, mold, and pests.

Those structural and system items come first, right after closing. For Cedar Ridge, that's the dock railing, the lower-level alarms, the well retest, and a clear exit from every bedroom.

The Consumer Product Safety Commission's vacation rental tips add the rest: CO alarms on every level, an extinguisher, anchored furniture, and drain covers. OP.6 builds these into the furnishing plan.

Both groups finish before photos, on a one-page sign-off.

left.head: Right after closing: structure and systems
items: Smoke and CO alarms disclosed, working, tested
Dock railing and lower-level alarms done
No blocked exits, exposed wiring, mold, or pests
Clean well retest
Instructions for the dock, lake, and stairs

right.head: During furnishing (OP.6): CPSC tips
items: At least one fire extinguisher
TVs and furniture anchored to the wall
Pool or spa drain covers, if there is one

slides.title: Forty-five days without guests cost Maya and Chris $4,885.50 in carrying costs
slides.side: Maya and Chris closed on day 0 and plan to launch on about day 45 (assumption).

side_box.label: The number to watch
side_box.text: If the permit takes longer, each extra month costs another $3,257.

slides.notes:
Maya and Chris closed on day 0. They plan to launch on about day 45. That's an assumption. Here's what those 45 days cost before a single booking.

Carrying costs keep running with no revenue. Their monthly PITIA on the DSCR loan is $2,557. PITIA means principal, interest, taxes, insurance, and any association dues. Utilities, internet, and trash are $450 a month. Software is $100 and the handyman retainer is $150. That's $3,257 a month, the same carrying cost we used in lesson 0.3.

Forty-five days is one and a half months. So that's $3,257 times 1.5, or $4,885.50. It's a simple prorated estimate. Your real first payment dates may differ, so check your closing disclosure.

The number to watch is the permit. If it takes longer than planned, each extra month costs another $3,257. That's why the permit application goes in on day 2, not after the furniture arrives.
slides.keyline: Launch timing is an assumption; other figures come from the Cedar Ridge example

slides.title: Between closing and the first guest, $39,840.50 leaves Maya and Chris's accounts
rows: PA.9 repairs paid by the buyers
**Cash out between closing and first guest**

box.label: What's left
box.text: The $142,688 total cash in already includes the $32,000 furnishing. $231,000 - $142,688 - $2,955 - $4,885.50 = $80,471.50 left.

slides.notes:
Now the one-time costs. The post-close repairs from due diligence total $2,955. That's the dock railing, the alarms, and the HVAC service. The seller handled the septic and well work before closing.

Furnishing is budgeted at $32,000. OP.6 covers how to spend it.

Add the $4,885.50 carry, and $39,840.50 goes out between closing and the first guest. Permit and tax registration fees aren't in this table.

Careful with the savings math. Cedar Ridge's total cash in of $142,688 already includes the $32,000 furnishing. It's the $110,688 cash to close plus $32,000. So don't subtract the furnishing twice.

Maya and Chris had $231,000 of liquid savings at the offer. Subtract $142,688, the $2,955, and the $4,885.50. That leaves $80,471.50, not counting anything saved since. Next, their set-asides come out of it.
slides.keyline: Launch timing is an assumption; other figures come from the Cedar Ridge example

slides.title: After their set-asides, only $2,379.50 is unallocated, so the plan leans on saving
slides.keyline: Figures from the Cedar Ridge example and earlier lessons
rows: Six months of essential household spending (0.3)
Two years of PA.9's weak case: 2 × $5,875

box.label: Below the cushion
box.text: That's under their $10,000 cushion. About $10,500 saved since the offer, at $3,500 a month (assumption), puts them back above it.

slides.notes:
Here are the set-asides that come out of the $80,471.50.

The property reserve is six months of PITIA, $15,342. The emergency fund is $51,000, six months of their essential household spending from lesson 0.3. The weak-year reserve is $11,750. PA.9's weak case is the pessimistic year, with lower rates and fewer booked nights. In that year the house falls $5,875 short of its costs and loan payments. PA.8's cash test holds two years of it.

Together that's $78,092, which leaves $2,379.50 unallocated. That's under the $10,000 floor they promised to keep after any surprise.

They still save about $3,500 a month. About three months have passed since the offer, so roughly $10,500 puts them back above the floor. The margin is thin, and it depends on that saving continuing.

If the permit runs late, each extra month comes out of the property reserve. That's what the reserve is for, but it leaves less for later surprises.

slides.title: A dated day 0 to 45 plan gives every task exactly one owner
rows: Reset lock codes; remove seller device accounts; condition photos (records only) and meter readings
Transfer electric, propane, internet, trash; set up autopay
Confirm insurance declarations, conditions met, loss-of-income terms with the insurer
File short-term rental (STR) permit application; register for lodging tax
Dock railing, alarms, HVAC service; handyman lines up the other vendors
Furnishing delivery and setup (OP.6); Chris helps on delivery days
Safety sign-off walk; the handyman walks with her
Listing and software setup (OP.1 to OP.5); publish once the permit row is done
First guest (assumes the listing was published and booked in time)
slides.notes:
Here's their day-by-day plan. It's an assumption, but the shape is what I'd copy.

Day 0, the day of closing, Maya resets the lock codes and removes the seller's device accounts. She takes condition photos for their records, not for the listing, and meter readings.

In the first few days, Chris moves the utilities and sets up autopay. Maya confirms the insurance terms with the insurer. On day 2, Chris files the short-term rental permit application and registers for lodging tax.

The handyman handles the railing, alarms, and HVAC between days 3 and 10. The lab retests the well on day 12. Maya runs furnishing from day 10 to 30.

The safety sign-off walk is day 30. Listing photos come on day 32. Chris builds the listing from day 30 to 44 and publishes once the permit row is done. Day 45 assumes it was published and booked in time.

Notice every row has exactly one name.

slides.title: Start the handoff packet with the property, coverage, permit, and utility facts
rows: Address, parcel, beds, baths, permitted capacity, size, year built
Names exactly as on deed, insurance, permit
Water main, well pump, UV, septic lid, panel, propane, HVAC filter size
Carrier, policy number, named insured, limits, deductibles, claim phone, renewal
Zone, policy yes/no, carrier, effective date
Permit number, holder, expiry; lodging tax account, filing frequency
Provider, plan, tested speed per room, router location
slides.caption: The written lesson adds a Source column for every field. Fill it in too.
slides.notes:
Here's the exercise: build the operations handoff packet and date it. Update the date every time you change it. If you haven't closed yet, fill it in for Cedar Ridge first, then copy the blank version for your own property.

The full packet has 21 fields. I've split it across two slides. This first half is the property itself.

The packet date and version. The property facts, including the permitted guest capacity from PA.9. The title owner and operator, spelled exactly as on the deed, the insurance, and the permit. A floor plan showing exits, shutoffs, the panel, and alarms. Where every shutoff and system lives, down to the HVAC filter size.

Then insurance, flood, permits and tax, utilities, and internet.

In the written lesson each field also has a source column, like the declarations page or the inspector's report. Fill that in too. Status is done or open. Date is the day you last confirmed the row.

slides.title: Finish the packet with the people, schedules, reserves, and every open issue
rows: Lock model, how codes are issued, vendor codes list, key holders
Outdoor cameras and noise monitor: location, disclosed; thermostat
Location in password manager; who has access
Cleaner, backup, handyman, septic, well, HVAC, plumber, electrician, pest, plow, trash, co-host
Room-by-room furniture and supplies (filled in OP.6)
Septic, well test, UV lamp, HVAC, alarm tests, roof check, gutters
Fire, CO, leak, power loss, dock injury, weather; who calls whom
Roof, HVAC, water heater, appliances, septic and well invoices
Property reserve, emergency fund, weak-year reserve, plus PA.9's roof sinking fund
Every row from the PA.11 log, with owner and due date
slides.notes:
The second half is about people and time.

Access and devices, including where the outdoor cameras and noise monitor sit and whether they're disclosed. Where the credentials live. Keep the credentials themselves in the password manager, not in the packet.

The contact list from the vendor slide. The inventory, which OP.6 fills in. A maintenance schedule built from the PA.9 findings: septic, well test, UV lamp, HVAC, alarm tests, the roof, and the gutters.

An emergency plan. OP.8 turns it into an SOP. The safety sign-off. Warranties and records. The budget reserves: the property reserve, the emergency fund, and the weak-year reserve, plus the roof sinking fund PA.9 placed inside the capital reserve.

And last, open issues. Every row from your PA.11 unresolved items log goes here, with its owner and due date. Store the packet where your cleaner, handyman, and co-host can read it.

slides.title: Don't publish the listing until the insurance, permit, and safety rows say done

gates.q: Does the insurance row say done?
gates.sub: Rental use, limits, conditions confirmed in writing.

gates.q: Does the permit row say done?
gates.sub: Issued, or confirmed in writing that you may list before issuance.

gates.q: Does the safety sign-off row say done?
Does every open issue have one owner and one due date?
gates.no: Assign one name and one date

slides.end: All yes: publish the listing. Update the packet version whenever a vendor, code, or policy changes.
slides.notes:
The packet has three rules. I've turned them into gates you check before you publish the listing.

The first rule is that the listing doesn't go up until three rows say done. Insurance, with rental use and conditions confirmed in writing. The permit, issued, or the licensing office confirmed in writing that you may list first. And the safety sign-off, signed and dated.

The second rule is that every open issue has one owner and one due date. 'We' is not an owner. If a row says 'we,' it belongs to nobody.

The third rule is about upkeep. Update the packet version whenever a vendor, a code, or a policy changes. A packet from three months ago with the old cleaner's number sends your next call to the wrong person.

slides.title: Five kinds of experts sign off on coverage, permit, tax, safety, and records
rows: Rental use, liability limits, deductibles, exclusions, loss of income, conditions met, flood, named insured
Permit issuance, holder's name, occupancy limit, whether you can list before issuance
Lodging tax registration and filing frequency
The safety and system items on your sign-off
Records and accounts to set up now, and the date the property is ready and available to rent (this date affects when depreciation can start)
slides.notes:
Here's who confirms what after closing.

Your insurer confirms rental-use coverage, the liability limits, deductibles, exclusions, loss-of-income terms, that the conditions are met, flood coverage, and the named insured. Get it in writing.

The local licensing office confirms the permit, whose name it's in, the occupancy limit, and whether you can list before it's issued.

The state or local tax agency confirms your lodging tax registration and how often you file.

A licensed electrician, septic inspector, or certified water lab confirms the safety and system items on your sign-off, as needed.

And your CPA confirms the bookkeeping records and accounts to set up now. The CPA also confirms the date the property is ready and available to rent. That date affects when depreciation, the yearly tax write-off for wear on the building, can start. Sam's PA.5 covers it, so don't guess the date.

slides.title: Bring specific outputs to each of Sam's demos, then OP.6 turns the budget into rooms
rows: **OP.1 Listing Creation Across Airbnb, VRBO & Booking.com and OP.2 2026 Listing Optimization** (Sam)
Permit number, guest capacity, safety disclosures
**OP.3 Building Your Direct Booking Website and OP.4 Tech Stack Architecture** (Sam)
**OP.5 Dynamic Pricing & Revenue Management for Owners** (Sam)
The PA.9 revised budget, including the $400 yearly permit renewal
**OP.6 Furnishing & Interior Optimization for an Owned Property** (Preston)
slides.notes:
The house is insured, connected, safe, and documented. Next come Sam's operations demos. I won't re-teach them here. Here's what to bring to each one.

OP.1 and OP.2 show the listing build. Bring your permit number, your real guest capacity, and your safety disclosures.

OP.3 and OP.4 connect the lock, the messaging, and the software. Bring your device list and your access plan from the packet.

OP.5 sets rates. Bring the PA.9 revised baseline, so your pricing targets use the real cost structure. For Cedar Ridge that means the $400 yearly permit renewal on top of the original budget.

Then I pick up again in OP.6, where the $32,000 furnishing budget turns into a room-by-room plan.

slides.title: Lock down coverage, access, and the permit clock in your first week of ownership
items: Pull your declarations page and check the nine insurance items against it.
Reset every lock code and remove the seller's device accounts.
File the short-term rental (STR) permit application, or confirm the date you will.
Start the handoff packet: fill in the date, property facts, and names.
slides.notes:
Four things to start this week.

First, pull your declarations page and check the nine items against it. Write down anything you need to ask the insurer.

Second, reset every lock code and remove the seller's accounts from each device.

Third, file the short-term rental permit application. If you can't file yet, find out exactly what's missing and put the date on your calendar. Every extra month of waiting costs Cedar Ridge $3,257.

Fourth, start the handoff packet. Date it, fill in the property facts, and write the names exactly as they appear on the deed, the insurance, and the permit.

That's the last acquisition lesson. Next is Sam's OP.1 Listing Creation. Bring your permit number, guest capacity, and safety disclosures. After Sam's OP.1 to OP.5, I pick up in OP.6 Furnishing & Interior Optimization.

slides.notes:
These are the sources behind this lesson.

Most of the platform rules come from Airbnb's own help center. That covers what AirCover includes and doesn't, the safety requirements, and the camera and device rules. It also covers where the permit number goes, and the host's responsibility for insurance, taxes, and permits.

The flood points come from FEMA and FloodSmart. The practical safety items come from the CPSC's vacation rental tips. The credentials point borrows from the CFPB's closing-scam guidance.

Each one was checked on September 25, 2026, through a search summary of the official page, because direct fetches were blocked. Airbnb updates its help articles often, so open them yourself before you set up your listing.

The Cedar Ridge figures come from the course's recurring example and earlier lessons. The 45-day launch and the day plan are assumptions.
